panels.title: The face we always see
body: The Moon turns once on its axis in the same time it takes to go once around Earth. That's why it always shows us the same face.
When it was young it spun much faster, but Earth's pull slowed it down until the two matched.
details: One trip around Earth, measured against the stars, takes 27.32 days; from full Moon to full Moon takes 29.53 days, because Earth moves round the Sun in the meantime (NASA fact sheet).

In this scene the Moon is drawn with an approximate tidal lock and no libration (the slight rocking that lets us see a little round the edges over a month), so surface features can sit several degrees from their true place.
This moment is chosen near the start of the scene so the first panel opens soon after play; nothing special happens at this time.
sources: NASA Science, Moon facts: "The Earth and Moon are tidally locked"; the same hemisphere faces Earth all the time; https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/ (accessed 2026-10-18)

NASA Science, Tidal locking: the young Moon spun faster, and its rotation slowed until one spin took the same time as one trip around Earth; https://science.nasa.gov/moon/tidal-locking/ (accessed 2026-10-18)

NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, Moon Fact Sheet: revolution period 27.3217 days, synodic period 29.53 days; https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html (accessed 2026-10-18)
Astraeus src/core/bodies/moon.ts, orientation limitations: approximate tidal lock, no libration

panels.title: The Moon is slowly drifting away
body: Every year the Moon moves a little farther from Earth, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
We know because Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon, and observatories still bounce laser beams off them today.
details: The Moon recedes by about 3.8 cm (1.5 inches) a year, measured by lunar laser ranging; NASA makes the fingernail comparison. NASA puts the drift down to gravitational (tidal) interactions between Earth and the Moon.
Reflector arrays were left by Apollo 11 (July 1969), Apollo 14 and Apollo 15.
This moment is the full Moon of 13 January 2025 at 22:27 UT (NASA phases table). Over the three months of this scene the drift is about a centimetre, far too small to see.
sources: NASA, Laser Beams Reflected Between Earth and Moon Boost Science (L. Shekhtman, 10 Aug 2020): "the Earth and Moon are slowly drifting apart at the rate that fingernails grow, or 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) per year"; https://www.nasa.gov/missions/laser-beams-reflected-between-earth-and-moon-boost-science (accessed 2026-10-18)

NASA/JPL, The Apollo Experiment That Keeps on Giving (24 Jul 2019): reflectors from Apollo 11, 14 and 15; the distance increases by 3.8 cm a year; https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/the-apollo-experiment-that-keeps-on-giving/ (accessed 2026-10-18)
NASA Goddard (F. Espenak), Phases of the Moon 2001 to 2100, Universal Time: full Moon 2025 Jan 13 22:27; https://eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov/phase/phases2001.html (accessed 2026-10-18)

panels.title: A red Moon in Earth's shadow
body: Early on 14 March, the Moon slides completely into Earth's shadow. It doesn't vanish: it glows a deep coppery red.
That light has passed through Earth's air, as if every sunrise and sunset on Earth were shining on the Moon at once. People across the Americas watched it for about an hour.
details: Greatest eclipse: 14 March 2025 at 06:58:41 UT. NASA's catalogue gives 06:59:56 in Terrestrial Dynamical Time (TD); minus Delta T of 75 s, that is 06:58:41 UT (catalogue of lunar eclipses, Espenak and Meeus, entry 09706: total eclipse, Saros 123, umbral magnitude 1.1784, totality 65.4 minutes, partial phases 218.3 minutes). The panel opens at greatest eclipse.

Totality ran from 06:26 to 07:31 UTC (NASA), about 65 minutes. NASA lists the eclipse as visible from Earth's western hemisphere; its decade table names the Pacific, the Americas, western Europe and western Africa.
The scene places the Moon from its ephemeris but does not draw Earth's shadow, so the Moon is not shown darkened or red.
sources: NASA Goddard (F. Espenak and J. Meeus), Catalog of Lunar Eclipses 2001 to 2100: 09706, 2025 Mar 14, greatest eclipse 06:59:56 TD (Delta T 75 s, so 06:58:41 UT), Saros 123, type T, umbral magnitude 1.1784, partial 218.3 min, total 65.4 min; https://eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov/LEcat5/LE2001-2100.html (accessed 2026-10-18)

NASA Goddard, Lunar Eclipses 2021 to 2030: 2025 Mar 14, 06:59:56 TD of greatest eclipse, total, Saros 123, totality 01h05m, visible Pacific, Americas, western Europe, western Africa; https://eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov/LEdecade/LEdecade2021.html (accessed 2026-10-18)

NASA Science, What You Need to Know about the March 2025 Total Lunar Eclipse: totality 06:26 to 07:31 UTC; "It's as if all the world's sunrises and sunsets are projected onto the Moon"; https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/moon/what-you-need-to-know-about-the-march-2025-total-lunar-eclipse/ (accessed 2026-10-18)
